newsitem.title: JAPAN: Deregulation forcing Japan's NTT to become tougher.
newsitem.headline: Deregulation forcing Japan's NTT to become tougher.

text.p: The opening of Japan's telecommunications market is slowly closing in on Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp, the world's biggest telecoms firm, accused for years of inefficiency and overpricing.
Stepped up activity by foreign and domestic competitors spurred by deregulation is eating into NTT revenues from both local and long-distance calls in the home market, analysts say.
The gigantic company, employing 185,000 workers, is shrinking itself to compete more efficiently with the upstarts but it will still have 150,000 workers by the year 2000.
"New entrants will certainly increase competition in the market. For NTT, it means a loss of market share, profit," said Barry Dargan, a senior analyst at SBC Warburg Securities Japan.
NTT's latest headache is likely to come from Japan's biggest international telecoms carrier, Kokusai Denshin Denwa Co Ltd, created in 1953 as government utility.

KDD said on Thursday it would invest 100 billion yen ($900 million) to lay an 8,500 km (5,300 mile) undersea optical fibre cable around three of Japan's main islands. The cable is expected to be in use by mid-1999.

Company president Tadashi Nishimoto told a news conference the cable would enable KDD to offer domestic long-distance call services cheaper than NTT. He said it would move into domestic services after the amendment of a law restricting it to international business. The amendment is expected by next summer.

NTT, also formerly a government-owned company, has for years relied on long-distance domestic services as its major source of income. In the year that ended on March 31, the long-distance service accounted for 75 percent of its parent operating profits.
Competition is coming from a new quarter as well.
Last week, the government announced that it will allow a cable television operator to offer telephone services using its fibre-optic network for the first time.
With their large-capacity cables already in place, the cable operators are thought to have the biggest potential to end NTT's virtual monopoly in the local market.
The cable group, Titus Communications, links Japan's Itochu Corp and Toshiba Corp with American phone group US West and communications conglomerate Time Warner Inc.
It said it planned to offer telephone services next July for 400,000 to 500,000 subscribers at rates significantly lower than NTT's.
"This is the first step in introducing competition in Japan's local telephone market," a Titus spokesman said.

In the government's deregulation steps announced late last year, the centrepiece is the abolition of business barriers that had restricted telephone operators to segmented services such as local, long-distance and international operations.
Only NTT is barred from international services, due to pending government discussions for splitting it up.
NTT is not sitting on the sidelines, however.

It is readying itself for competition by launching a low-cost, Internet-like network dedicated to data transmission, which is expected to strengthen its earnings structure by boosting profits from local calls and giving it a chance to move into new business areas.
